newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters strike wears on with no talks set.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters strike wears on with no talks set.

text.p: The nationwide strike against United Parcel Service dragged through a second day Tuesday, with no talks scheduled between management and the Teamsters union despite efforts by the Labour Secretary to bring the two sides back to the bargaining table.
As the strike idled UPS facilities, it spelled more trouble for American businesses and consumers, who were forced to seek other ways to ship their packages and documents.

Thousands of members of the Teamsters union, including drivers, package sorters and loaders, walked picket lines from Maine to California, as about 50,000 UPS managers and non-union workers scrambled to keep some of the company's massive operations moving.

With the union and UPS far apart on the use of part-time workers, pay and pensions, Labour Secretary Alexis Herman called Teamster President Ron Carey and United Parcel Service Chairman James Kelly to try to persuade them to consider returning to the bargaining table for the first time since the strike began on Monday.
"I spoke to both parties privately by telephone this afternoon and urged them both to go back to the bargaining table," she said in a statement.
Both sides said they are willing to meet, but there was no sign of a break in the impasse.

"We're prepared to meet any time, anywhere, with a mediator or without one to negotiate a contract that provides good jobs for working families," Carey said at a rally outside a UPS facility in Burtonsville, Md.
The company, meanwhile, said it would not alter its proposal in light of Herman's request.
"We are ready to go back to the table. But our position hasn't changed about our offer. We've made our last, best and final offer," UPS spokesman Norman Black said.

UPS had less success petitioning the White House to order the strikers back to work under the Taft-Hartley Act, which gives the president authority to end work stoppages that threaten national health and safety.
"Every telephone conversation the White House has with both parties we are urging them to get back to the table," White House spokesman Barry Toiv said on Tuesday.
U.S. President Bill Clinton has so far ruled out direct federal intervention in the strike.
The strike began hours after UPS negotiators refused to budge from the same offer during a last-ditch bargaining effort on Sunday night.

UPS, which lost $50 million during a partial one-day strike in 1994, said 10 percent or less of its usual 12 million packages a day were being delivered and that only a few facilities were operating normally. It stopped taking orders from consumers and shifted its focus to express and international shipments.
"If you're looking to send something to grandma, this is not the time," UPS spokeswoman Kristen Petrella said.

Union officials said the strike had crippled the company. "UPS is pretty much buttoned up. Packages in the system are drying up and the strike appears to be virtually 100 percent effective," Teamsters spokesman Rand Wilson said.
The 185,000 Teamsters who sort and load packages, haul shipments and drive the company's familiar brown vans and trucks account for two-thirds of the work force at the company.

Deliveries inside and between European countries remained unaffected by the strike. But Petrella said UPS was no longer guaranteeing deliveries on parcels bound overseas from inside the United States.
At picket lines, five more Teamsters were arrested for violence, bringing the number of arrests near UPS facilities to more than a dozen, police said.

The walkout, the first national strike in UPS' 90-year history, is also the largest in the United States this decade. It pits a wealthy $22.4 billion private company using more part-time workers against a union whose members are angry about the practice, as well as other issues. Part-time jobs pay $9 an hour on average after two years vs. $20 an hour for full-time jobs at UPS.

As the world's largest parcel delivery company, Atlanta-based UPS controls four-fifths of the nation's package shipment business and says deliveries amount to more than 6 percent of the U.S. gross domestic product.
The strike is also a gamble for Teamster President Ron Carey, who is facing powerful opposition in the union and allegations of fund-raising abuses in his re-election campaign last year.

The Independent Pilots Association, which represents 2,000 UPS pilots, was still supporting the strike by keeping members off the job. UPS consolidated its air shipment services at the Louisville hub, which on Monday night handled 40 UPS flights piloted by managers and 29 chartered flights, 30 percent of its normal capacity.
With UPS facilities idled, its rivals have stepped in to pick up some of the slack.

Memphis, Tenn.-based Federal Express Corp. said its volume has increased to nearly peak holiday levels since the strike began. Daily volume jumped to about 3.5 million to 4.0 million packages a day, compared with normal August volume of about 2.8 million.
"The system is challenged and stretched beyond normal capacity. We're approaching holiday-level capacity," said Jess Bunn, a spokesman for Federal Express.
